options.outcomeLabel: You're oriented toward healing, not just moving on

genderInsight.male: Bringing wounds to God as healer shows a widower who is letting grief draw him closer rather than push him away. This posture of surrender, 'make me whole first', is exactly right.
genderInsight.female: A healing-oriented prayer life means you're inviting God into the grief rather than trying to heal independently. This surrender is the deepest form of trust.

options.text: As distant. I believe He is there but I struggle to feel His presence or direction specifically about this area of my life
options.outcomeLabel: You believe but feel God is far away

genderInsight.male: God feeling distant after losing your wife is a faith crisis many widowers face silently. The man who prayed for his wife's healing and watched her die has legitimate questions for God, bring them honestly.
genderInsight.female: Feeling distant from God after losing your husband is a wound on top of a wound. The spiritual loneliness of grief deserves focused attention, perhaps through a grief-sensitive pastor or spiritual director.

options.text: I am honestly angry or confused at God. The ending of my marriage shook my faith and I have not fully recovered
options.outcomeLabel: Your divorce created a spiritual crisis

genderInsight.male: Anger at God after your wife's death is one of the most honest prayers a widower can offer. God can handle your rage, but staying in spiritual crisis while trying to build a new marriage puts that marriage on shaky ground.
genderInsight.female: Spiritual crisis from losing your husband is a real and valid faith test. The anger, confusion, and questioning are legitimate, and they need resolution, not suppression, before you can build again.

questions.text: When you consider loving again as a Christian, with the loss you have experienced, what is the state of your heart before God?

options.text: I have peace. I believe God honors my late spouse's memory AND wants good things for my future. These are not in conflict
options.outcomeLabel: You feel spiritually at peace about your divorce

genderInsight.male: Spiritual peace about loving again means you've resolved the 'am I betraying her?' question before God. Many widowers struggle silently with this, your freedom here is a gift.
genderInsight.female: Peace about remarriage after loss means you've wrestled with the 'am I betraying his memory?' question and found freedom. This spiritual clarity will undergird everything.

options.text: Mostly at peace, but moments of doubt surface, sometimes wondering if God fully approves of me trying again
options.outcomeLabel: You're mostly at peace but have lingering doubt about loyalty

genderInsight.male: Wondering if moving on dishonors your late wife is deeply normal for widowers. Bring that tension to God honestly, He's not keeping score on your grief timeline.
genderInsight.female: Lingering doubt about whether God wants you to love again is common for widows. Your vows were 'til death do us part', and death did part you. There is freedom here.

options.text: Unsettled. Carrying guilt or theological confusion about whether remarriage is right for me after losing my spouse
options.outcomeLabel: You're uncertain whether remarriage honors your late spouse's memory

genderInsight.male: Feeling caught between loyalty to your late wife and desire for new love is one of the deepest spiritual tensions a widower faces. This is worth processing with a pastor or counselor.
genderInsight.female: If you feel that loving again betrays your vows or God's purpose, this spiritual conflict will block your ability to fully invest in someone new. It deserves focused attention.

options.text: I feel spiritually stuck, like loving again would somehow betray my late spouse, my vows, or God's purpose in my suffering
options.outcomeLabel: You feel spiritually paralyzed by loyalty and grief

genderInsight.male: Spiritual paralysis about remarriage means the theological and emotional work hasn't been done yet. Your late wife would likely want you to find love again, and so does God.
genderInsight.female: Feeling that loving again betrays your late husband, your vows, and God is a heavy burden. You are not bound to loneliness as a tribute. Please talk to someone who understands grief and faith.

questions.text: You imagine building a new home with a future spouse. When you picture the emotional atmosphere you want to create, what is the honest gap between that vision and who you are today?

options.text: The gap is small. I am already living many of the values I want in my future home. I am not waiting for marriage to practice them
options.outcomeLabel: You're already living the healthy remarriage vision

genderInsight.male: Already living the values you want in a future home means your late marriage taught you what matters and you've carried those lessons forward. As a widower, this continuity of character is reassuring to a new partner.
genderInsight.female: A small gap between your vision and your reality means the good things from your marriage have been preserved and expanded. Your next husband enters a life already shaped by intention.

options.text: I can see the vision clearly but I know I still have work to do. Some of my patterns do not match my aspirations yet
options.outcomeLabel: You see clearly where you want to be and what needs work

genderInsight.male: Seeing the vision while naming the gap shows a widower who learned from his marriage without pretending he perfected everything in it. This honesty and aspiration together are attractive and safe.
genderInsight.female: Clear vision with honest acknowledgment of remaining work is the most realistic widowed position. Your late marriage was real, with both beauty and struggle, and your next one deserves the same honesty.

options.text: I want something beautiful but I am not sure I know how to create it. I did not see it modeled growing up
options.outcomeLabel: You have a vision but lack real examples to follow

genderInsight.male: Wanting a healthy home without a clear model may mean your first marriage didn't provide the template you need. As a widower, you may have had a beautiful marriage but still carry family-of-origin patterns that need attention.
genderInsight.female: Not having a clear model for what you want to build means you'll need intentional learning, from healthy couples, from counseling, from books. The desire without the map requires extra navigation help.

options.text: I am scared I will recreate what I came from. I do not trust myself to build something different
options.outcomeLabel: You fear repeating your family's patterns

genderInsight.male: Fear of recreating old damage is painful self-awareness. As a widower, this fear may connect to patterns from your childhood rather than your marriage. Name what you're actually afraid of repeating.
genderInsight.female: Fear of repeating damage shows you understand the stakes. But fear alone doesn't build, it freezes. Pairing the awareness with intentional growth turns the fear into motivation.
